articles.title: He Left The Top Of The Supreme Court For A Job He Thought Mattered More
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

John Jay was the first Chief Justice of the United States, but he found the job so underwhelming — a Court that heard only a handful of cases, plus miserable circuit-riding duty — that in 1795 he resigned outright. What did he leave the nation’s top judicial post to go do?

Hint: While still on the bench, he negotiated the 1794 Jay Treaty with Britain which was so reviled that he was denounced as a traitor and burned in effigy up and down the coast.

The post He Left The Top Of The Supreme Court For A Job He Thought Mattered More appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: The Rise Of The Legal Engineer: The New Job 40 Years In The Making
articles.content:
Every so often, a new job appears that makes you wonder: Where did that come from?
Add this one to the list: Legal Engineer.
If you haven’t heard the term before, you’re not alone. Five years ago, relatively few lawyers would have known what one was. Today, legal engineering is emerging as an important new discipline at the intersection of law and technology.
So what exactly is a legal engineer?
The simplest answer may be this: someone who understands how lawyers work and knows how to turn that work into technology-enabled systems.
A lawyer does the legal work.
A legal operations professional helps manage the business and processes surrounding the legal work.
A legal engineer asks a different question: Can we build a better way to do the work?
Enter AI
For decades, lawyers have been surrounded by technology. But there is an enormous difference between using technology and actually redesigning legal work around it.
AI has made that distinction considerably more important.
According to the 2026 Legal Industry Report from 8am™, 69% of legal professionals report personally using Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude for work-related purposes. AI for law firms is quickly becoming part of day-to-day work.
For a profession historically cautious about new technology, that rate of adoption represents a dramatic increase from the less than one-third (31%) indicated in their 2025 report.
In one year, AI went from something most lawyers weren’t using to something nearly four out of five were using in some capacity.
But buying an AI platform and figuring out how a law firm should actually use it are two very different things.
Someone has to understand the legal problem. Someone has to understand the workflow. Someone has to determine where AI should — and shouldn’t — be involved.
Someone has to configure and test the system and determine whether the resulting work product is actually any good.
Increasingly, that someone is the legal engineer.
What Do They Actually Do?
Suppose a corporate legal department handles hundreds of routine contracts.
Traditionally, a business person sends something to Legal. A lawyer reviews it. Emails go back and forth. Somebody finds the right template. Somebody tracks approvals. Somebody follows up.
A legal engineer looks at that process and asks: Why are we doing it this way?
Could intake be automated? Could the answers determine which agreement gets generated? Could AI identify provisions requiring lawyer review? Could routine agreements proceed without ever touching a lawyer’s desk?
The lawyer still determines the legal standards and handles the difficult judgment calls.
The legal engineer builds the machine around them.
That can mean designing workflows, automating documents, configuring AI systems, connecting applications, analyzing data, and testing the finished product.
An Idea Close to 40 Years in the Making
Interestingly, the concept isn’t entirely new.
Legal futurist Richard Susskind was writing about the “legal knowledge engineer” in his doctoral work in 1986 and in Expert Systems in Law in 1987.
The technology was primitive by today’s standards, but the underlying idea was remarkably predictive: someone would have to take knowledge that existed inside lawyers’ heads and translate it into systems that computers could use.
For decades, that remained largely a very interesting idea.
AI to the Rescue
Suddenly, the technology began catching up with the prediction.
There is no cookie-cutter path to a career as a legal engineer.
Some legal engineers are former practicing lawyers. Others come from legal operations, knowledge management, paralegal roles, software development, or product management.
The skill set is unusually hybrid. You need enough understanding of legal work to recognize what lawyers are actually trying to accomplish, an understanding of processes and workflows, and sufficient technical fluency to figure out how technology can accomplish the task.
What may matter most is something lawyers are already trained to do: Take a complicated problem, break it into its component parts, and figure out how the pieces fit together.
Not to be Confused With Prompt Engineering
A legal engineer isn’t simply someone who is good at writing prompts for Claude, ChatGPT, etc.
Prompting may be one tool in the toolbox. But the larger job is systems thinking.
What is the legal team trying to accomplish? Which decisions require human judgment? Which don’t? What can be automated? Where can AI make mistakes? And how do we create something that lawyers will actually use?
Those questions aren’t principally about technology.
They’re about understanding legal work.
Which May Be Why Lawyers Are So Well Suited to It
For all the discussion about AI eliminating legal jobs, legal engineering illustrates the other side of technological disruption.
New technology doesn’t merely eliminate jobs.
It creates new ones.
AI isn’t simply changing what lawyers do, it is creating demand for people who can stand between law and the machines increasingly being used to deliver it.
What Qualifications are Needed
While requirements vary, based on our research, the ideal legal engineer candidate increasingly looks like this:
• At least three years practicing law, with firsthand knowledge of how legal work actually gets done.
• Technical fluency, including almost always a working knowledge of Python, AI tools, and APIs, along with automation and no-code/low-code platforms such as Zapier, Make, and n8n.
• Workflow and process-design skills — the ability to identify repetitive or inefficient legal work and figure out how to automate it.
• The ability to translate between lawyers and technologists — understanding the legal problem and communicating what needs to be built to solve it.
• Curiosity and problem-solving instinct — the inclination to ask, “Why are we doing it this way, and can technology do it better?”
What About Compensation?
Depending on experience and employer, legal engineers with legal and technical expertise can earn roughly $150,000 to $300,000+, with the highest-paying roles at Am Law 100 law firms and legal AI companies.
To learn more about nonlegal careers for lawyers and lawyers who have already successfully left the practice of law, the EXJ Community is a good place to start.
The authors of The Great Escape column, Neil Handwerker and Kimberly Fine, are the founders of exjudicata.com, a platform designed to help lawyers move to nonlegal careers. They just launched a new related platform, the EXJ Community, the first ever peer-to-peer network of non-practicing lawyers.
The post The Rise Of The Legal Engineer: The New Job 40 Years In The Making appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Scholastica, Law Reviews, And Gatekeepers Of Academic Prestige
articles.content:
Let us tell the story of a suit against Match.com. In 2019, the Federal Trade Commission sued “Match Group, Inc. (Match), the owner of Match.com, Tinder, OKCupid, PlentyOfFish, and other dating sites, alleging that the company used fake love interest advertisements to trick hundreds of thousands of consumers into purchasing paid subscriptions on Match.com.” A separate class action lawsuit also alleged that “keeps thousands of inactive, fake and fraudulent profiles on its dating site to mislead customers about their chances of finding a mate.”
This isn’t an article about matchmaking for love. This is about matchmaking between journals and authors. And much of that matchmaking is done on a site called Scholastica.
Once upon a time, professors had to use the U.S. Postal Service to submit articles, cover letters, and resumes to as many journals as they wished. This was a lengthy, inefficient, and costly process. Eventually a digital platform called Express-O came on the market and provided a one-stop mechanism for submitting everything to one web site and then distributed the packet electronically (for a fee) to as many law reviews as the professor wished. Professors and their administrative assistants breathed a sigh of relief. It also made it much easier to flood hundreds of law reviews with submissions with very little effort.
Eventually, law reviews embraced electronic submission as their preferred or exclusive method of submission. The journals’ electronic mailboxes filled up while their physical mailboxes emptied out. For a variety of reasons, over the past 12 or so years, journals began including Scholastica as an additional option, and Express-O went out of business in 2021.
Today some law journals have their own individual submission portals with various idiosyncratic requirements about format, anonymization, abstracts, tables of contents, AI use, etc. Some allow direct submission via email. Most law reviews rely on Scholastica for their exclusive or preferred submission portal. The law reviews then respond to the authors with an eventual acceptance or rejection through the platform and notify Scholastica when they are “open” for submissions and when they are “closed” for the season or academic year. Lucky professors often leverage the first acceptance by asking for a substantial deadline to respond and contacting higher-ranked journals that have not yet responded for an expedited decision before the initial deadline. Scholastica, like Express-O before it, held forth the promise of a single, relatively efficient (but not cheap) method of sending up a draft law review article and accompanying materials to as many journals on the platform at one time, receive one or more acceptances, and publish with the “best” (highest-ranked) journal to make an offer.
That promise is increasingly in jeopardy. Sure, some professors continue to play the game successfully, but it’s a radically smaller group in recent submission cycles. Even famous-named folks are having trouble placing articles in the top 30 law reviews. And worse, the problem of overwhelmed law review editors seems to have trickled down to the law reviews at the lower end of the rankings. In short, many folks have faced more than two article submission seasons this year without any placements.
There are more law review articles than ever before. For any individual article, cost is the only real deterrent to submitting to all journals and law reviews where there is a chance of being accepted (for example, presumably authors don’t submit an environmental law article to a specialty tax journal). Some higher-end journals suggest they are screening over 3,000 articles (while only having a max of 20 slots for those articles). Those are bad odds.
Part of the problem is also AI. I’ve written about law review editor use of AI screens before. Depending on the nature of the backlog, the problem promises to get worse.
What exactly are we law professors getting for our (or our institution’s) money? And how do we cope with a system where we have to hit “submit” without knowing when or even if a journal will ever consider an article on the merits, i.e., actually read it?
Submitting to a law review in Scholastica that signals it is “open” doesn’t tell much information. When journals are open, that could mean they are fully open or just need to fill one or two slots. Sometimes the journal is actually full and hasn’t yet submitted that information to Scholastica. The authors do not know, which means they could be paying for a very low or zero payoff lottery ticket.
If a journal signals “open,” there may be no guarantee it is really open. What incentives do journals that are closed have to signal closed on Scholastica after they are filled? In other words, is there any penalty for a journal signaling open when it isn’t, causing authors to submit to the journal in error? If not, are authors paying a fee for phantom open journals?
Scholastica seems to recognize this: “One of the most frustrating experiences for an author is to send their article to a law review only to find out that the editors are no longer reviewing submissions.” At $7.35 per submission, it can add up.
Other data that would perhaps allow authors to gauge their risk is also not available. What’s the acceptance rate of the journal over time?
I worry, much like in the Match.com case, the love for our articles may be DOA, yet we’re paying for submitting the article to the grave. Scholastica could create greater information for law review submissions, greater transparency, and all those good things, but I wonder if it has an incentive to do it if it costs them submission fees.
Scholastica, if you’re listening:
1. Make the journals disclose any screening that isn’t based on scholarly content. AI screens ought to be disclosed. Should authors not rush to send our drafts that are timely until we make it pretty and not falsely signal AI?
2. Make Scholastica like digitized parking stalls. Show how many slots are available so that authors can make decisions to risk trying to place their articles there or look for greener pastures.
3. Make the number of submissions to that journal known as well. If the journal has 5,000 submissions, authors can surmise they aren’t going to read all of those. In an ideal world, law reviews would disclose what proxies they use (psst … some of the data shows exactly what we all suspect)
For everyone else (including the FTC and state AGs):
1. It’s time to think about how to inject more competition into the process to ensure higher-quality and less-costly ways to submit scholarship for publication. Right now, we have a high-priced inefficient system and a separate set of individual submissions for many of the most highly ranked journals.
2. It’s also time for more scrutiny of the limited and potentially misleading disclosures by Scholastica and the journals themselves.
3. I would love a lot more data than that, but I don’t really think that’s Scholastica’s job. For example, if a law review has almost never accepted a law review article from someone not at a T10 school (or at least from there), should we continue to waste time and money submitting there to feed their anti-intellectual screening mechanisms and elitism?
4. And in a side note to law professors: it also might be a good time to have a discussion about the purpose of legal scholarship. I always thought it was to better humanity through illumination — in law, that is based upon understanding of the literature that came before us and improving upon it (or rejecting it) in a thoughtful and transparent manner. I could be wrong. Maybe it’s even time for a random submission lottery and a “Hunger Games”-style tournament to replace reprints from highly ranked journals as trophies and digital downloads as their modern equivalent.

articles.title: This Legal Writing Expert Wants Lawyers To Embrace AI
articles.content:
Ed. note: Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day.
The closest analogy [for AI] is a U.S. Supreme Court clerk at your elbow: astonishingly well-read, relentlessly available and capable of an extraordinary turnaround. …
That’s why the clerk analogy is so apt. A clerk doesn’t relieve a judge of judgment. A clerk makes more judgment possible.
— American legal scholar and lexicographer Bryan Garner, writing for the ABA Journal, explaining why lawyers should view artificial intelligence as an exceptionally capable law clerk rather than a substitute for their own judgment. AI may research, analyze, and produce work at remarkable speed, but the lawyer must still decide what’s accurate, relevant, and persuasive. As Garner puts it, when “used properly,” AI “keeps the lawyer in command while making the work quicker, tougher and better.”
Staci Zaretsky is the managing editor of Above the Law, where she’s worked since 2011. She’d love to hear from you, so please feel free to email her with any tips, questions, comments, or critiques. You can follow her on Bluesky, X/Twitter, and Threads, or connect with her on LinkedIn.
The post This Legal Writing Expert Wants Lawyers To Embrace AI appeared first on Above the Law.
